cases.description: When a newly created JsonSchema instance has never had a required validator assigned, the internal requiredValidator field remains null, so hasRequiredValidator() should return false.

After injecting a non‑null JsonValidator (e.g., via reflection or a public setter) into the private requiredValidator field, hasRequiredValidator() must recognise the presence of the validator and return true.

A schema that defines an object type and contains a non‑empty "required" array should cause JsonSchema.initializeValidators() to create a RequiredValidator, therefore hasRequiredValidator() must return true.
When the schema is an object but does not declare a "required" keyword, initializeValidators() must not create a RequiredValidator, so hasRequiredValidator() should return false.
Even if a "required" keyword is present, it is only meaningful for object types. For a non‑object type (e.g., string) the RequiredValidator should not be instantiated, resulting in false.

After a schema that initially creates a RequiredValidator (hasRequiredValidator() = true), the private requiredValidator field is set back to null via reflection (resetRequiredValidator = true). The method must now return false.

A child schema created with createChildSchema() that does not define its own "required" keyword must not inherit the parent’s RequiredValidator. Hence, hasRequiredValidator() on the child should be false.

Both parent and child schemas define a "required" keyword. After creating the child schema via createChildSchema() and initializing its validators, the child must have its own RequiredValidator, so hasRequiredValidator() returns true.
